The story behind an idea

First and last: the serial position effect

From a list we remember the beginning and end best. The middle gets lost.

As early as the late nineteenth century, Hermann Ebbinghaus noticed that when learning lists of syllables he remembered the first and last ones best. In the 1960s, Murdock and later Glanzer and Cunitz studied it in detail.

Two effects in one

The first words are remembered better because we have had more time to rehearse them and they pass into long-term memory: this is the primacy effect. The last ones are still fresh in short-term memory: this is the recency effect. If people are asked to recall the list after a few seconds of distraction, recency disappears but primacy remains.

It has practical uses: in a presentation, put the important point first and repeat it at the end; when studying, change the order of topics so the middle ones are not always learned least well.

References

  1. Murdock, B. B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(5), 482–488.
  2. Glanzer, M. y Cunitz, A. R. (1966). Two storage mechanisms in free recall. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 5(4), 351–360.
